title: The lamps of the sky
told: a sakhi, a traditional story of Guru Nanak

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when did something last make you stop and just say “wow”?
options: then you already know today’s word. listen.
then this story is for you. listen.
that’s okay. this one might help. listen.

steps.line: Long ago, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana, a Muslim musician, walked to Puri, a temple town by the sea in eastern India.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: At dusk the priests lifted golden trays of lamps, flowers and incense, and waved them in worship. It’s called aarti.

steps.q: Everyone joins the aarti. What do you think Guru Nanak does?
o: Joins the priests at the front
steps.why: He stayed outside. Not to be rude. He had something even bigger to show them.

steps.line: Guru Nanak didn’t join in. The puzzled priests came out and asked him why.

steps.q: He points up at the sky and sings. In his song, what do you guess the stars are?
steps.why: The pearls. The sky is the tray, the sun and moon are its lamps, and the stars are scattered pearls.

steps.line: He pointed up and sang. The sky is the tray. The sun and moon are the lamps. The stars are the pearls.

steps.q: Why didn’t Guru Nanak need a tray of lamps?
o: The whole sky was already worshipping
He wanted his own way of praying
steps.why: To him the whole world was already offering its light. Nothing needed adding.

steps.line: Mardana played, and Guru Nanak kept singing: sandalwood on the wind is the incense, the forests are the flowers. The whole world is already doing aarti.

steps.q: Sikhs still sing this song. When?
steps.why: It’s part of Kirtan Sohila, the prayer sung at night. In many gurdwaras it’s also sung as the Guru’s own aarti.

steps.line: Sikhs still sing that song every night. And when something is bigger than words, they say Waheguru: wow, the teacher.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Before his travels, Guru Nanak’s first words after a great experience became famous. What were they?
steps.why: After three days lost in the river Bein, tradition says, he came out saying, “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” Walking to Puri with Mardana, a Muslim, he lived it.

say: here’s what i love. guru nanak didn’t look away from worship. he looked up, and saw the whole sky joining in.
that wonder is inside the name sikhs say for god. waheguru: wahe, wow; guru, the teacher. when words run out, wow is the answer.

steps.q: Sikhs say Waheguru at good news and at hard news. From this story, why might one word fit both?
o: It points past the mood, to something bigger
It’s a polite way to fill a silence
It works as both thanks and a sigh
steps.why: It isn’t a report on your mood. Like the song under the sky, it’s wonder at what is bigger than you.

today.say: tonight, step outside or to a window for one minute and look up. if you like, let one word go out with your breath: waheguru. or simply: wow.
options: the sun, the moon, the stars. the whole tray. enjoy it.
that’s fine. the sky will still be there, lamps lit.

tomorrow.line: a father gives his son twenty rupees to make a good deal. the son comes home with nothing, and a whole new idea.

card.keepWhy: The whole sky is already lit. Wow.
